notes.meaning: Paul begins by defending his freedom as a Christian and his authority as an apostle. He had seen the risen Jesus in person on the road to Damascus, which was an essential proof of being an apostle. The church in Corinth itself existed because of his hard work in the Lord.

Even if believers in other places doubted Paul's calling, the Corinthians had no reason to do so. Their own conversion and spiritual life were the seal, or official mark of proof, that God had truly sent him. Their existence as a church proved his ministry was genuine.

Paul uses courtroom language to address his critics, speaking as if he were on trial. His official defense against those who judged him was simply the evidence of what God had accomplished through him in Corinth.

Paul asks whether he and his co-workers have the right to receive food and drink from the church. Apostles were entitled to be cared for by the people they taught, even though Paul chose not to claim this benefit.

Paul asks if he has the right to be married to a Christian woman and have the church support her on his travels. Other apostles, the Lord's brothers, and Peter all traveled with their wives. Paul had the same freedom to marry, though he gave it up to focus on his mission.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some traditional Roman Catholic writers have understood this verse to speak of holy women who traveled with the apostles to care for their daily needs, rather than wedded wives.

notes.meaning: Paul asks whether he and Barnabas are the only church leaders expected to work manual jobs to buy their own food. Every other apostle received financial support from the churches, so Paul and Barnabas had that same right.

Paul points to ordinary life to show that workers deserve support. Soldiers do not pay for their own equipment, farmers eat grapes from their vineyards, and shepherds drink milk from their sheep. In the same way, ministers should be supported by the people they serve.
Paul asks whether this principle comes only from human reason or common practice. He explains that God's written Law in the Old Testament teaches the exact same rule of fairness.

The Law of Moses commanded that an ox should not wear a muzzle while walking over grain to separate it. While God cares for animals, this law was meant to teach a larger lesson about human workers. Those who work to provide food have the right to eat from that work.

God gave this ancient command for the benefit of His human servants. A worker who plows a field and a laborer who threshes grain both work with the fair hope of receiving a share of the harvest. God expects His ministers to have that same hope of being fed.

Paul compares his preaching to planting valuable spiritual seeds in the hearts of the Corinthians. Since he gave them eternal spiritual blessings, it was not too much to expect basic earthly food and clothing in return.

Other teachers in Corinth were already receiving support from the church, so Paul had a far greater claim as their spiritual father. Yet he refused to take money from them so that no one could say he preached for profit and thereby hinder the gospel.

Under the Old Testament law, the priests and Levites who served at the temple received their food from the offerings brought to the altar. Everyone knew that religious workers were supported directly by their holy duties.

In the same way, Jesus commanded that those who preach the good news should make their living from their ministry. This was not a human invention, but a clear command given by Christ Himself for His church.

Even though Paul had a clear right to be paid, he chose not to use it. He was not writing to ask them for money now, because he would rather die of hunger than lose his proud joy of offering the gospel without charge.

Paul could not brag simply because he was a preacher, because God had placed a sacred obligation on him. Jesus had called him directly, and Paul knew serious trouble awaited him if he failed to preach.

If Paul had chosen this mission purely by his own idea, he might have expected personal wages. Instead, God drafted him into service and entrusted him with a sacred duty as a steward, leaving him no choice but to obey.
Paul's special reward was the joy of offering the good news completely free of charge. By giving up his lawful right to be paid, he made sure he did not use his authority in a way that hurt anyone.

Even though Paul was a free man who belonged to no human master, he voluntarily made himself like a slave to all people. He willingly set aside his personal rights so that he could lead as many people as possible to Christ.

When Paul was with Jewish people, he respected their customs and observed the Law of Moses so he would not offend them. He knew keeping these ceremonies could not save him, but he followed them to help his Jewish listeners welcome the gospel.

When Paul lived among Gentiles who did not have the written Law of Moses, he adapted to their daily ways. He was careful to add that this did not make him lawless, because he was always under the moral law of love and obedience to Christ.

When dealing with believers who had tender or troubled consciences about food and special days, Paul accommodated their feelings with great care. He adapted himself to all kinds of people in every lawful way so that at least some would be saved.
Paul made all these personal sacrifices for the sake of the good news. His greatest desire was to see people saved and to share with them in the eternal blessings of the gospel.

Paul points to the famous athletic games held near Corinth, where many run in a race but only one athlete wins the prize. He urges Christians to live their faith with the same full effort and dedication as a runner chasing victory.

Athletes in the games endured months of strict training, denying themselves rich foods and comforts just to win a leafy crown that soon dried up and died. Christians have a far greater reason for self-control, because their reward is an imperishable crown of eternal life.

Because Paul knew exactly where he was headed, he did not run aimlessly. He compares himself to a focused boxer who aims every punch carefully at his opponent rather than swinging wildly and hitting only the air.

Paul treated his physical body like an athlete in hard training, bringing its desires into complete subjection. He was determined that after announcing the rules and preaching to others, he would not fail the test and be disqualified from the prize.

differ.view: Ministers and believers face a real danger of falling away into sin and being eternally lost if they do not persevere in holy living.
True believers are kept safe in salvation by God's grace; Paul was speaking of being disapproved or losing his reward and fitness for ministry, not losing eternal life.
